newsitem.title: FRANCE: New French minister gets tough on alcohol, smoking.
newsitem.headline: New French minister gets tough on alcohol, smoking.

text.p: Bernard Kouchner, France's new Health Minister, said he will introduce new requirements for health warnings on cigarette packets and will not tolerate an alcohol brand using the World Cup football tournament as a shop window.

In a speech made on Monday, but released on Tuesday, at a conference of health professionals, Kouchner seemed to indicate the new left-wing government's health policy would be less conciliatory towards World Cup sponsor Anheuser-Busch, which makes Budweiser beer.
Kouchner said a law had existed in France since 1991 to tackle alcohol and tobacco abuse.

"I confirm that the 1998 World football Cup will not give rise to any twisting of this law. It would be intolerable that this sporting event, which will be closely followed by the youth of our country, should serve as a shop window for a brand of alcohol. This will not be the case," he said.
France's Loi Evin bans all advertising for cigarette or alcohol brands, and outlaws the broadcasting of sporting events sponsored by such brands.
Anheuser-Busch had lobbied the previous centre-right government to obtain a compromise to allow it to put up billboards for Budweiser at stadiums hosting World Cup events in France next year.
The issue had not been resolved when the left government won power at the June 1 election.

A solution favouring the American brewer might have involved giving World Cup stadiums some kind of extra-territorial status, a government source said, adding that the final word on the issue would come from the new Sports and Youth Minister, Marie-George Buffet.
Kouchner also signalled a tougher stance about the warnings cigarette manufacturers put on their packets.
"I also announce that I will take measures in the next few days on the labelling of cigarette packets, to make prevention messages more readable," he said.

Last month, a Paris court fined cigarette makers Seita and Rothmans for having health warnings that distorted the meaning of the labelling law. Seita was fined 300,000 French francs ($50,900) and Rothmans 200,000 francs.
"I was particularly shocked by attempts, condemned by the courts, to distort these messages. These must be less ambiguous and easier to read," Kouchner said.
-- Sue Landau, Paris Newsroom, 4221 5452 ($ = 5.883 French Francs)
